event: Tuesday: frost on the shingle at dawn; you and Shiv swim to the buoy and back through the steam.
The red-cheeked second-year reads out your time: five minutes. Shiv whistles, impressed.
On the shingle Shiv rubs your arms through the towel. "Penhallow today. Essays back. Scared?"
You say yes. Shiv shrugs: hers is three pages and one joke, and she'd do it the same again.
At breakfast Bea makes you eat toast. "You can't get an essay back on an empty stomach."
Nine: Penhallow's study; the essays come back in a stack, each marked in green ink.
Penhallow explains for you: alpha, beta, gamma, with plus and minus. "An early alpha is rare."
She hands them round. Priya beta plus, delighted. Shiv beta, unbothered. Lin beta plus, pink.
Kit's and Amara's both say beta plus; they look at each other's pages and both look away.
Yours says alpha minus, in green, at the top; and at the bottom one question: "Whose wanting?"
You stare at it. Penhallow is watching you over her glasses. "Think about it," she says. "Friday."
Kit leans over, sees the alpha, and says under her breath, "Of course you did." She's smiling.
Priya squeaks and hugs you sideways; Lin touches your sleeve under the table.
Penhallow spends the hour on mending: is a mended cup the same cup? The room splits in two.
Shiv says it's a new cup with an old cup's habits; Penhallow laughs and gives her shortbread.
Amara laughs about her beta plus, lightly, all the way down the tower stairs.
Eleven: the Foundations lecture; Amara's seat in front of yours is empty for the first half.
After, you go to the bathroom by the Long Room; someone is crying in the end cubicle, quietly.
You know the gold watch on the wrist resting on the cubicle door handle. "Amara?"
The crying stops. "Go away, Freckles," Amara says, thick-voiced. You sit on the floor outside.
"I do this," she says through the door. "After every test. Even when I win. Every single one."
You tell her she argued a room flat in four minutes last week; you saw it. A wet laugh.
"That's the trick," says Amara. "You make it look easy. Then you come in here."
She asks, through the door, what you do when you're frightened. You say: swim in a freezing mere.
"Mad," says Amara. "Utterly mad." But she's laughing properly now, and the bolt slides back.
She comes out at last, eyes red, and fixes her face in the mirror, fast and expert, in silence.
"Keep this to yourself," she tells your reflection. "I'm good at that," you say.
Amara kisses your cheek, quick and fierce, smelling of cocoa butter. "Alpha minus. Damn you."
Lunch: Amara sits with Priya and is dazzling and loud; she catches your eye once, and winks.
Two: practical; the cracked cups again; this time you breathe out longer, and your seam closes.
It closes all the way to the base, a faint line left; the demonstrator holds it to the light. "Yes."
Bea's cup gets warm again; she glares at it, and then laughs until she has to sit down.
Lin mends hers on the second try, and the line left is so fine it looks drawn in pencil.
At the end bench Kit mends hers, back to the room; Amara, two benches down, watches Kit's back.
Amara looks at Kit's turned back a long moment, frowning, as if a sum won't come out.
Dusk in the empty Practice Hall; you sit on the front bench and look at Kit, openly, from the start.
Kit stands mid-floor, coat off, sleeves pushed up, and breathes out before she starts.
The sigil; the word; her hand stops in the air, and her face whitens. You hold her eyes. "Out."
She breathes out. The glim comes: small, wavering, then steadier, a pale bead of light. It holds.
You count aloud for her, softly: one, two, three, four, five. On six it goes out.
Kit lowers her hand slowly. "Five," she says. "Watched." Her voice shakes, and her eyes shine.
She does it twice more; the third time it holds to eight before it goes.
On the bench after, her head on your shoulder, Kit says: "Tomorrow, two pairs of eyes."
"Whose?" you ask. Kit is quiet a long time. "Bea's," she says. "She's decent. She said so."
You tell her about the alpha, and the question; Kit reads it twice in the dim hall.
"Whose wanting," she says. "Penhallow always asks the one you can't answer yet. Granny said."
You walk her to Ashcombe's door across the frosted quad; she kisses you on the step, slower tonight.
At Thornfield you knock on 15 and tell Bea; Bea sits up straight in bed. "Me? Really? Me?"
"I'll sit very still," Bea promises. "I'll be the stillest person in the world." She's beaming.
She asks to see the essay; she reads the alpha, and whoops, and the girl in 16 bangs on the wall.
Room 1 is dark; it's Tuesday, one of Yusra's infirmary nights.
In 14 you take the essay out, and read the green question again under your lamp: whose wanting?
You think of Alan in the chair by the back window, and of this body, and can't say which.
You fall asleep with the essay on your chest and the question still open.
A day at Hollowmere ends.
